summary: Clarify Retry-After semantics on overload errors (429/503) and whether requests are billed when overload-protected errors occur
description:
Customer asks:
1) How should they interpret the Retry-After header when they receive overload-related 429/503 responses? Is it seconds? Is it required or advisory?
2) Do overload errors count against billed usage / token usage? They saw intermittent 503s during burst traffic and want to understand whether they are charged for failed requests.

Context:
- Customer recently added automatic retries in their client for both /v1/chat/completions (streaming) and /v1/embeddings.
- They observed a mix of 429 and 503 during a predictable spike (top-of-hour batch jobs).
- They want guidance compatible with OpenAI-style error objects (they use OpenAI SDK in one service and Redwood SDK in another).

Impact:
- Confusion about recommended retry/backoff behavior.
- Concern about unexpected charges during outage-like periods.

Requested outcome:
- A clear, support-approved explanation for Retry-After + backoff recommendations.
- A clear statement on billing behavior for overload-protected errors (and any edge cases for streaming).
comments:
2026-01-14 10:12 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Acknowledged question. Looping in Product/Billing for billing semantics and SRE for Retry-After guidance.

2026-01-14 10:38 PT — Brian Murphy (API error semantics)
Retry-After is emitted for overload-protection responses (429/503) and is an integer number of seconds. It is intended to be honored by clients to avoid retry storms. For OpenAI-compat endpoints we also include the standard error structure, but Retry-After remains the canonical backoff hint.

2026-01-14 11:05 PT — Cole Summers (Quotas/Billing hooks alignment)
Billing: requests that terminate with an overload-protection response (e.g., 429/503 with Redwood overload codes) are not billed as successful usage. For token-billed endpoints we bill on tokens actually generated/returned. If a request is rejected before inference starts, there is no usage to bill.
Edge case: streaming requests where some tokens were already successfully emitted to the client prior to a disconnect are billed for tokens emitted. If the stream never starts and we return an overload response, no tokens are emitted and nothing is billed.

2026-01-14 11:22 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Follow-up for clarity: if they get a 503 without any response body (timeout/connection reset), does that count as overload-protected? They mentioned seeing occasional upstream timeouts.

2026-01-14 12:01 PT — Brian Murphy
If they see a structured JSON error with Redwood overload code + Retry-After, that is the overload-protected response. Timeouts/connection resets without that payload are not “intentional load shedding” and should be treated as an internal failure mode; they should open a ticket with request IDs so we can trace. (Separately, as rollout progresses we expect fewer ambiguous timeouts and more deterministic 429/503 with codes.)

2026-01-14 12:25 PT — Dev Patel (Support) — Draft response to customer (for review)
- Retry-After is seconds; we recommend exponential backoff with jitter; treat Retry-After as minimum delay.
- Do not retry immediately; cap max retries; consider respecting idempotency and timeouts.
- Billing: overload-protected errors are not billed as usage; streaming only bills for tokens actually delivered.

2026-01-15 09:10 PT — Nikhil Sharma (Hosted API PM)
Approved wording. Please include distinction: 429 often indicates request throttled/admission control (fairness/tiers), 503 indicates temporary capacity pressure or regional saturation. Guidance is the same: respect Retry-After and use jitter.

2026-01-15 09:42 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Sent response to customer with specifics + links to retry guidance doc. Asked them to confirm whether the 503s they’re worried about include Retry-After / structured body. Requested 2–3 example request IDs for any “empty 503/timeout” cases.

2026-01-16 14:18 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Customer confirmed most errors include Retry-After and Redwood error payload; those were their main concern. They had a small number of timeouts but will send request IDs separately if it continues. Marking resolved.

Customer-facing response (as sent):
---
Retry-After:
- Retry-After is an integer number of seconds and indicates a minimum delay before retrying.
- We recommend: wait at least Retry-After, then use exponential backoff with jitter (avoid synchronized retries), and set a max retry count.
- Please avoid immediate/zero-delay retries, especially for burst traffic.

429 vs 503:
- 429 typically indicates admission control / throttling to protect fairness and prevent cascades.
- 503 indicates the service is temporarily unable to accept the request due to overload/capacity pressure.
- In both cases, Retry-After is the best signal for when to retry.

Billing:
- If a request returns an overload-protection error response (e.g., 429/503 with a structured error payload + Retry-After), that request is not billed as successful usage.
- For streaming: tokens are billed only for tokens successfully emitted to the client. If the stream never begins and we return an overload error, no tokens are emitted and there is no token usage billed.

If you ever see ambiguous timeouts/connection resets without a structured error payload, please send request IDs and timestamps—those are not expected under load-shedding and we’ll investigate.
---
resolution: Provided support-approved guidance on Retry-After semantics (seconds; treat as minimum backoff; add exponential backoff + jitter) and clarified billing behavior (overload-protection error responses not billed as successful usage; streaming bills only for tokens emitted). Shared docs links and requested request IDs for any remaining ambiguous timeouts.
